narration.text: Let's start with the simplest case — a diagonal matrix. Grid and circle, ready to transform.
For a diagonal matrix, the eigenvectors point along the axes. The eigenvalues are right there on the diagonal.
Lambda one is 2, lambda two is 3. The circle stretches into an axis-aligned ellipse.
Now a harder case — an upper triangular matrix. The eigenvalues are still on the diagonal, but the eigenvectors tilt.
Watch the eigenvectors — they stay on their own lines during the transformation. That's the defining property.
What about a rotation matrix? Let's apply a ninety-degree rotation.
Every vector changes direction. No vector stays on its own line.
That means no real eigenvalues. The eigenvalues are plus and minus i — complex numbers.
Complex eigenvalues signal pure rotation. The magnitude tells you the angle.
Let's see all three side by side. Diagonal, triangular, rotation — transforming simultaneously.
Eigenvalues tell you how much. Eigenvectors tell you which direction. Together, they decode the matrix.
No real eigenvectors? The transformation is fundamentally rotational.
Where do eigenvalues come from? The characteristic equation: determinant of A minus lambda I equals zero.
This single equation unlocks every eigenvalue of every matrix. It's the master key.
From geometry to algebra and back — that's the power of eigenvalues.
